summary: A function pointer holds the address of a function so that the function to call can be chosen at run time. C uses them for callbacks, dispatch tables, state machines and vtable-style interfaces, since the language has no lambdas or virtual methods. You see them in `qsort`, `signal`, `pthread_create`, kernel driver operation tables and interrupt vectors.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: A function pointer is a variable that holds the address of a function, so the function to call can be chosen at run time. Functions live in the code segment and have addresses just like data; the name of a function, used in an expression, decays to a pointer to it. Function pointers are how C expresses callbacks, plug-in behaviour, dispatch tables, state machines and object-style interfaces, and they underpin library APIs such as `qsort`, `bsearch`, `signal`, `atexit` and `pthread_create`.
bullets: **Problem they solve**: C has no lambdas, virtual methods or generics. Passing a function pointer lets generic code call behaviour supplied by the caller.
**Core cost**: an indirect call. It is slightly slower than a direct call and usually blocks inlining.
**Core risk**: calling through a pointer of the wrong type is undefined behaviour, and a corrupted pointer is a classic exploitation target.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Declaration**: `int (*fp)(int, int);` reads as fp is a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning int. The parentheses around `*fp` are essential: `int *fp(int, int);` declares a function that returns `int *`.
**Taking an address**: `fp = add;` and `fp = &add;` are equivalent, because a function name decays to its address.
**Calling**: `fp(2, 3)` and `(*fp)(2, 3)` are equivalent. The first form is more common.
**Function type is part of the type**: return type and parameter types must match. `int (*)(int)` and `int (*)(long)` are incompatible.
**Typedef**: `typedef int (*binop)(int, int);` makes declarations readable: `binop table[4];`.
**Callback**: a function pointer passed to other code that calls it back later, often with a `void *` user-data argument.
**Dispatch table**: an array of function pointers indexed by an opcode, command or state.
**No arithmetic**: you cannot add to, subtract from, or take `sizeof` of a function; pointer arithmetic on function pointers is not allowed.
**Null**: a function pointer can be NULL, and testing `if (fp)` before calling is the normal optional-callback idiom.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: The compiler resolves a direct call to a fixed address at link time. For a call through a pointer it loads the pointer value into a register and emits an indirect call (`call *%rax` on x86-64, `blr x0` on AArch64). The CPU's indirect branch predictor guesses the target; a correct guess costs a few cycles, a wrong one costs roughly 15 to 20 cycles of pipeline flush. The example below shows declaration, assignment, call, an array of pointers, and passing a pointer as an argument.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Plain pointer**: `int (*f)(int);` to one function of that signature.
**Array of function pointers**: `int (*ops[4])(int, int);` or with a typedef, `binop ops[4];`. Used for jump tables and command dispatch.
**Pointer to function returning a pointer**: `char *(*f)(const char *);`.
**Function returning a function pointer**: `binop pick(char c);` is easiest with a typedef. Without it: `int (*pick(char c))(int, int);`.
**Struct of function pointers (vtable)**: group related operations to emulate interfaces. The Linux `struct file_operations` has `read`, `write`, `ioctl`, `mmap` and more; each driver fills its own.
**Callback with context**: `void register_cb(void (*cb)(void *ctx), void *ctx);`. The `void *` carries state because C has no closures.
**`const` function pointer**: `int (*const fp)(int) = f;` means the pointer itself cannot be reassigned.

**Dynamic symbols**: `dlsym` returns `void *` for a function. ISO C does not allow converting `void *` to a function pointer, but POSIX requires it to work, and the usual cast is `*(void **)(&fp) = dlsym(h, "name");` or a direct cast that compilers accept with pedantic warnings.
**Compared with alternatives**: a `switch` or if-chain is faster for few fixed cases and inlines; a table is better when the set is large, runtime-extensible or data-driven.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Size**: a function pointer is one machine word, 8 bytes on 64-bit targets, though the C standard does not require it to be the same size as `void *`.
**Call cost**: about 1 to 3 cycles when predicted correctly, 15 to 20 when mispredicted. A direct call can be inlined to zero cost.
**Dispatch table**: O(1) lookup `table[i](args)`, versus O(n) for an if-chain, and equal to a compiler-generated jump table for a dense `switch`.
**`qsort` cost**: an indirect comparator call per comparison, about n log2 n calls. For hot loops a type-specialised sort, or inlined comparison, can be 2 to 5 times faster.
**Memory**: a vtable shared by all instances costs one pointer per object (like C++), while embedding each pointer in every struct costs 8 bytes per operation per object.
**Mitigations**: Spectre variant 2 hardening (`retpoline`, indirect branch restricted speculation) makes indirect calls noticeably slower, so kernels reduce them on hot paths.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Misplaced parentheses**: `int *f(int)` is a function returning a pointer, `int (*f)(int)` is a pointer to a function.

**Calling with the wrong signature**: casting a function pointer to an incompatible type and calling through it is undefined behaviour, even if it appears to work (it breaks with different calling conventions, WebAssembly and control-flow integrity).
**Calling NULL or uninitialized pointers**: crashes at address 0 or at a random address. Initialize to NULL and test optional callbacks.
**Dangling pointer to a dead function**: a pointer into an unloaded shared library (`dlclose`) is invalid.
**Comparator bugs in `qsort`**: returning `a - b` for ints overflows. Use `(a > b) - (a < b)`.
**Unsafe `void *` casts**: `qsort` passes `const void *`; cast to the real element type inside the comparator, and match `const` correctly.

**Security**: function pointers stored in writable memory (heap structs, the GOT, vtables) are targets for overwrites. Hardening includes RELRO, stack canaries, `-fcf-protection` and control-flow integrity.
**Different calling conventions**: on Windows 32-bit `__stdcall` and `__cdecl` pointers are not interchangeable.
**Callbacks without context**: a global variable stand-in makes code non-reentrant and non-thread-safe; add a `void *ctx` parameter instead.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Standard library**: `qsort(base, n, size, cmp)`, `bsearch`, `atexit(fn)`, `signal(sig, handler)`, `sigaction` and `pthread_create(&t, NULL, start, arg)`.
**Kernel and drivers**: `struct file_operations`, `struct net_device_ops`, `struct inode_operations` are vtables filled by each driver; syscalls dispatch through the `sys_call_table` array.
**Embedded systems**: interrupt vector tables are arrays of function pointers; bootloaders jump to an application via a function pointer cast of its reset vector.
**Interpreters and VMs**: opcode dispatch via a table of handlers (threaded code) and plugin systems loaded with `dlopen`/`dlsym`.
**GUI and event loops**: libraries such as GTK and libuv register callbacks for clicks, timers and socket events.
**State machines**: each state is a function returning the next state function, or an array indexed by state.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **Declare a pointer to a function taking an int and returning a char pointer.** `char *(*fp)(int);`.
**What is the difference between `fp = f` and `fp = &f`?** None; the function name decays to its address.
**Difference between `int *f(int)` and `int (*f)(int)`?** Function returning `int *` versus pointer to function returning `int`.
**How do you implement callbacks with state?** Pass a `void *` user pointer along with the function pointer.
**Why use a function pointer table instead of switch?** O(1) dispatch, runtime extensibility, data-driven design.
**Can you do arithmetic on function pointers?** No; only assignment, comparison and calls.
**How does C emulate polymorphism?** A struct holding function pointers (a vtable) that each implementation fills.
**Write the comparator for qsort of ints.** `static int cmp(const void *a, const void *b) { int x = *(const int *)a, y = *(const int *)b; return (x > y) - (x < y); }`.

subtopics.title: Declaring and reading function pointer types
subtopics.summary: Parsing the declarator from the name outward.

sections.body: Start at the identifier and read outward, preferring the parentheses first. In `int (*fp)(int, int)`, fp is a pointer (`*`), to a function (`(int, int)`), returning int. In `void (*signal(int, void (*)(int)))(int)`, signal is a function taking an int and a pointer to a function (int to void), and returning a pointer to a function (int to void). The standard trick for readability is a typedef: `typedef void (*handler_t)(int); handler_t signal(int, handler_t);`. Tools such as `cdecl` translate between English and C declarations.
sections.code:
typedef void (*handler_t)(int);
handler_t signal(int sig, handler_t h);   /* far easier to read */

sections.body: Note a few shapes that confuse readers. `int (*arr[3])(int)` is an array of three pointers to functions. `int (*(*pp))(int)` is a pointer to a function pointer. A pointer to a function taking another function pointer, such as `void apply(int a, int b, int (*op)(int, int))`, reads naturally once the inner type is a typedef. Practise by building the declaration from the name outward, then verify with the compiler.

`qsort` is generic over element type, so it needs the element size and a comparator. The comparator receives two `const void *` pointing at elements and returns negative, zero or positive. Cast them to the right type, compare without subtraction overflow, and keep the function free of side effects. For sorting an array of structs by one field, the comparator derefs to the struct type.

subtopics.title: Dispatch tables and jump tables
subtopics.summary: Replacing long if/switch chains with an array.

sections.body: When commands map to handlers, an array indexed by opcode avoids a chain of comparisons. Bound-check the index first and leave NULL for unsupported entries. Designated initializers make the table self-documenting and robust to reordering. This is the shape of interrupt vectors, syscall tables and bytecode interpreters.

C callbacks cannot capture variables, so the registration API takes a `void *ctx` that the library hands back on every call. The callback casts it to the real type and reads or updates state. This keeps code reentrant and thread-safe without globals. The same pattern appears in `pthread_create(..., start, arg)`, `qsort_r` (glibc, BSD with a different argument order, C11 Annex K `qsort_s`) and event loop APIs.

Group related operations into a struct of function pointers and give each object a pointer to its table. Callers invoke `obj->ops->read(obj, buf, n)` without knowing the concrete type. Implementations differ per driver or backend. This is the pattern behind Linux VFS (`struct file_operations`), `FILE` layers in libc replacements, SQLite's VFS and many embedded HAL layers. It costs one extra pointer load per call and gives clean separation, easy mocking in tests and run-time substitution.

subtopics.title: Returning function pointers and state machines
subtopics.summary: Functions that pick or return behaviour.

sections.body: A selector can return a pointer to the chosen function, and a state machine can encode each state as a function that returns the next state. Both are much clearer with a typedef. A self-referential state type needs a struct wrapper or a `void (*)(void)` cast because C cannot declare a function type that returns itself directly.

subtopics.title: Safety and security
subtopics.summary: What can go wrong with indirect calls.

sections.body: A wrong-signature call is undefined behaviour. A function pointer in a writable object is a target: overwriting it through a buffer overflow redirects control flow. Defences include keeping vtables in read-only memory (`const struct ops`), full RELRO so the GOT is read-only after startup, stack protectors, `-fcf-protection` (Intel CET indirect branch tracking), and clang's `-fsanitize=cfi` which checks the call signature before each indirect call. Validate indices before dispatch and never take a function pointer from untrusted input without checking it against a known table.

subtopics.title: Performance considerations
subtopics.summary: When an indirect call is worth it.

sections.body: A direct call to a small function is inlined and often vanishes. An indirect call is opaque to the optimizer, adds a branch predictor entry and may mispredict if the target varies. In a loop that calls the same pointer repeatedly the predictor does well; in a loop with a pointer that changes randomly it does poorly. Strategies: hoist the call out of the loop, specialise the hot loop per case with a macro or a `static inline` template, or sort work by target. Profile with `perf stat -e branch-misses` before optimising.

subtopics.title: Emulating member functions with a struct
subtopics.summary: A C struct cannot hold a function, but it can hold pointers to functions.

sections.body: You can declare data members in a struct but not define functions inside it. Store function pointers instead and give each one an explicit first parameter pointing at the object, since C has no implicit `this`. A constructor-style function fills in the pointers. The call looks like method syntax, `r.area(&r)`, but the object must still be passed explicitly. This is the same mechanism as the vtable pattern, with the table embedded in every object instead of shared.

subtopics.title: Arrays of function pointers and menu-driven programs
subtopics.summary: Index into a table instead of branching.

sections.body: A table such as `int (*farr[])(int, int) = { add, sub, mul, divd };` lets you run any operation by index: `farr[0](10, 5)` gives 15, `farr[1]` gives 5, `farr[2]` gives 50, `farr[3]` gives 2. Menu-driven programs read a choice, range-check it, and call the table entry. Each function must share the exact signature, so protect special cases inside the function, for example `divd` returning an error value when the divisor is zero rather than dividing.

subtopics.title: Properties and rules at a glance
subtopics.summary: What a function pointer is and is not.

sections.body: A function pointer points into the code segment, not at data. It requires the exact signature of its target, though it can be reassigned to any function with that signature. The function name behaves like a constant function pointer, so `&` is optional on assignment. No arithmetic is allowed: `fp++` is an error. It can be stored in variables, arrays and structs, passed to functions and returned from them. A mismatched assignment is a compile-time type mismatch warning or error, and forcing it with a cast leads to undefined behaviour on the call.

takeaways: `int (*fp)(int, int);` is a pointer to a function; without the parentheses it is a function returning a pointer.
A function name decays to its address, so `fp = f` and `fp = &f` match, and `fp(x)` equals `(*fp)(x)`.
Use a typedef for any non-trivial function pointer type to keep declarations readable.
Callbacks need a `void *ctx` argument to carry state because C has no closures.
Arrays and structs of function pointers give O(1) dispatch tables and vtable-style interfaces.
Calling through an incompatible function pointer type is undefined behaviour; initialize to NULL and check optional callbacks.
Indirect calls cost a few cycles when predicted, about 15 to 20 when mispredicted, and block inlining.
